analysis.one_liner: Writes a 2020 EPA rule into law to limit states' power to block pipelines and other projects over water quality.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee and its water subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a federal law called the Clean Water Act, a company that wants a federal permit for a pipeline or similar project must first get a certificate from the affected state (or tribe) saying the project won't violate water quality standards. In 2020 the EPA issued a rule shortening the deadlines for that review and narrowing what states may consider. This bill would make that rule permanent federal law, so states could not easily delay or deny permits for natural gas pipelines, coal operations, or power lines based on concerns like downstream greenhouse gas emissions.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies building natural gas pipelines, power lines, and other energy and infrastructure projects, because states would have a narrower scope and shorter window to review and block their permits. Its findings argue this means cheaper, more reliable energy for consumers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes the July 2020 EPA 'Section 401 Certification Rule' permanent law, locking in narrower limits on what states and tribes may review and shorter deadlines for them to act on permit certifications [S2][S3].

Its stated purpose is regulatory certainty for pipelines, coal production, and electric transmission lines, which its findings call vital to affordable energy and to road-building projects in the national interest [S3].

The findings argue that states had been denying water quality certifications for reasons beyond water quality, such as downstream greenhouse gas emissions, and that lack of natural gas transport infrastructure contributes to higher energy prices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: States and Indian tribes would lose much of their current authority to review or deny federally permitted projects that discharge into their waters, including the ability to weigh climate-related effects. Communities that rely on state water quality protection would bear the risk of weakened local review; the bill contains no offsetting compensation or alternative protections.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently narrows the main tool states and tribes have under Section 401 of the Clean Water Act to protect their own waters from federally permitted projects, and it limits the time they have to complete reviews [S2][S3].
It would prevent states from considering downstream greenhouse gas emissions when deciding whether to certify a project, a use of Section 401 the bill's own findings say states have relied on [S3].

Supporters of preserving state authority would argue the bill shifts a cost of energy infrastructure onto the states and communities that host it, without those states' consent, and locks in a 2020 rule rather than allowing the EPA to revise it through the normal regulatory process [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers pipeline and transmission developers faster, more predictable permitting and claims consumer benefit through lower energy prices, but its cost falls directly on state and tribal authority to protect local waters, and the consumer savings are indirect and uncertain. Weighing a permanent restriction on the states' principal Clean Water Act check against a hoped-for price effect, the design favors project applicants over the governments and communities that host the projects.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then a subcommittee, no hearing or vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 28, 2022, by Rep. Ted Budd with two Republican cosponsors and referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where no further action was recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and tribal governments that kept their full Section 401 authority to review and reject federally permitted pipelines and other projects, since the restriction was never enacted. Groups that wanted the rule codified gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Ted Budd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to enact the 2020 EPA Section 401 Certification Rule into law.

for.name: Reps. Alex Mooney and Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill attracted no additional cosponsors.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat with the committee and its Water Resources and Environment subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill drew no Democratic support in a House where Democrats held the majority.

industries.industry: Natural gas and oil pipeline developers
industries.note: The bill would shorten and narrow state reviews of their federal permits, letting them build with less risk that a state denies certification over water or climate concerns. The trade-off for nearby communities is reduced state power to protect local waters.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel producers (natural gas and coal)
industries.note: The bill's findings name natural gas pipelines and coal production as beneficiaries of easier certification, since blocked certifications have stalled fuel production and transport projects. Cheaper transport is claimed to lower consumer energy prices.

Transmission lines and road projects would get faster, more predictable Section 401 certification, which the bill says serves the national interest. Faster interconnection can also support renewable energy buildout, so the effect on the public is less one-sided than for pipelines.

These governments would permanently lose the broad scope and open-ended review period they currently use under Section 401, including consideration of downstream emissions. Their loss of authority is the direct cost of the bill.
